# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L296


# Vulnerability details

When a project is launched, all associated ILOPools get launched. This process requires an ILOPool to mint the pre-calculated liquidity in the uniswap v3 pool and sending the required amount of tokens to the uniswap pool from within the uniswapV3MintCallback(). 

This will fail if the ILOPool contract does not have enough SALE_TOKEN because the transfer of this token will fail. There is no check anywhere to force the project admin to send required SALE_TOKEN amount to the ILOPools while initializing an ILOPool.

This means while the project and the ILOPools have been initialized and investors are locking their raise tokens in the contracts, the ILOPool contract might not even have any amount of SALE_TOKEN, because that is completely dependent on the project admin's wish. 

Eventually, when the launch time arrives and the project has not sent any SALE_TOKEN, launching will fail. 

## Impact
Project can intentionally not send any SALE_TOKEN to any deployed ILOPools, which will cause launch to fail. Investors who had locked their raiseToken liquidity will need to wait for the whole "pre-launch investing duration" + refund deadline until they can finally get back their tokens.

The default refund deadline is 7 days, and if we assume 1 month of pre-launch duration, the investors' funds get locked for 37 days, in return for nothing.

Investors face opportunity loss, and lose gas money, while they could have simply invested these funds to earn yield somewhere else. 

Project launch can also fail due to other reasons, like not reaching softCap, but that's a reasonable risk already known to the investors and independent of possible rugs. While the issue presented here is unreasonable. 

## Proof of Concept
launch() calls [addLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L296) => calls [pool.mint()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/base/LiquidityManagement.sol#L48) => this will initiate a callback to the uniswapv3mintcallback function [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/base/LiquidityManagement.sol#L27) => which involves [transferring tokens to the pool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/base/PeripheryPayments.sol#L33).

The token transfer here will fail if there are no Sale tokens in the ILOPool contract. 


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Force the project admin to transfer at least maxSaleAmount of SALE_TOKEN to every ILOPool they initialize. This can be done in the ILOManager.initILOPool() function. 

Any remaining amount of SALE_TOKEN will anyways get refunded to the admin at launch via _refundProject().

```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L173

# Vulnerability details

```_isBlacklisted``` is used to block suspected addresses from buying VULT tokens during the whitelisted period. According to the readme, this is done to remove any suspicious addresses that the admin might detect. But the protection is ineffective when self-whitelisting is enabled because such a malicious actor can have many addresses with which they can whitelist themselves repeatedly, and interact with the pool to buy VULT tokens.  

Also, when admin calls ```setBlacklisted()``` to blacklist an address, the malicious actor can simply front-run the admin's call to utilize their whole ```maxAddressCap``` and get the VULT tokens transferred to themselves, before the setBlacklisted call actually gets executed. In such a situation, there will be no effect of the blacklist as these token holders can easily use/transfer their VULT tokens after the whitelist period has ended, so they do not lose anything.


## Impact
Suspicious actors will be able to acquire hoard of VULT tokens and there is no effective way to stop them, and the blacklisting protection against this is ineffective. These actors can freely transfer these VULT tokens after the whitelist period has ended.

## Proof of Concept
The hook used to check whitelist logic is only called if the whitelist period is still running (ie. whitelist contract address has not been set to zero) :

``` 
function _beforeTokenTransfer(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override {
        if (_whitelistContract != address(0)) {
            IWhitelist(_whitelistContract).checkWhitelist(from, to, amount);
        }
        super._beforeTokenTransfer(from, to, amount);
    }
```
so even blacklisted actors can access the tokens they acquire maliciously.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove the self-whitelisting functionality and only allow the admin to add whitelisted addresses. Another solution can be to blacklist an address forever such that the tokens remain locked with them forever and any transfers revert, this way after getting blacklisted they will lose out on the VULT tokens as well as the ETH used to buy them.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The setRefundDeadlineForProject() function is used to set a project's refund deadline to an abrupt value, and is only callable by the ILOManager owner. 

It doesn't make sense to allow ILOManager owner to change a project's refund deadline. This has a range of impacts :

1. Refund deadline can abruptly be changed to any time without the project's will
2. Since it is not callable by project admin, projects are forced to use the default deadline and can never change the deadline
3. Should have a check that new refund deadline is still > project.launchTime, otherwise it will mess up the whole timeline

4. The most serious impact is this : It can be used by the ILOManager owner to prevent projects and their investors from withdrawing their liquidity indefinitely. If the project is not launching, everyone depends on refund deadline to get their funds back. It can be changed anytime for any project, even just before it was supposed to end.

This is a serious problem because investors' funds might be withheld indefinitely and get stuck in the contract.


## Proof of Concept
Project can only claim refund if refund Deadline has passed : [ILOManager.claimRefund()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L201)

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The refund deadline should not be configurable by anyone after the project has been initialized once. Allow projects to set a custom refund deadline ( that is >= DEFAULT_DEADLINE_OFFSET) during initialization.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L41


# Vulnerability details

When the pool is just launched, there are no price observations, which means that the price will be calculated as the initially fed value of sqrtPriceX96. As the trading activity starts, the spot price will be very volatile. The TWAP will be meaningless and prices returned will be highly manipulatable. This is because the twap period will depend on the time difference between block.timestamp and the  oldest observation present in the Observations array of Uniswap V3 Pool. 

Even after the first TWAP window has passed, and there are enough recorded observations to be able to calculate a meaningful 30-minute TWAP price, it will be using the haphazard prices (that were recorded before in the volatile trading activity) to find the average price. 

This means at least for the first TWAP window, as well as the following few hours, the TWAP prices returned will be unreliable and some users might be allowed to buy more than deserved amount of VULT tokens because of the calculation in UniswapV3Oracle.peek(), at the expense of other less sophisticated users buying from the pool.


## Impact

This will lead to a token sale where early hour participants with knowledge of sophisticated manipulation strategies can get an edge over the max VULT that can be acquired with the same amount of ETH, which they can later sell for profit.

Token sale opportunity should be equal to all users based on an accurate and reliable TWAP price. Additionally, users who acquire more than deserved VULT tokens via manipulation can become disproportionate holder of VULT. 

## Proof of Concept

Here, longestPeriod is the time difference between the current timestamp and the oldest recorded observation still present in the observations array(see [OracleLibrary.getOldestObservationSecondsAgo()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L75)). When it is smaller than 30 minutes, the consult() function will use this smaller duration. These conditions are true until the first TWAP window after launch passes.

```
    function peek(uint256 baseAmount) external view returns (uint256) {
        uint32 longestPeriod = OracleLibrary.getOldestObservationSecondsAgo(pool);
        uint32 period = PERIOD < longestPeriod ? PERIOD : longestPeriod;
        int24 tick = OracleLibrary.consult(pool, period);
        uint256 quotedWETHAmount = OracleLibrary.getQuoteAtTick(tick, BASE_AMOUNT,      baseToken, WETH);
        // Apply 5% slippage
        return (quotedWETHAmount * baseAmount * 95) / 1e20; // 100 / 1e18
    }
```

Thus, the TWAP returned will essentially be a volatile spot price for the initial duration.  

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To counter this, after a pool is initialized, the price derived from initial liquidity needs to be maintained for the whole of the first TWAP window, ie. for the first 30 minutes after the pool is launched. This will ensure that on the first swap, a reliable price gets recorded as an observation for the whole twap window, based on which a reliable twap price can be guaranteed for the early period, even for the first participants.

This can be done by only allowing the VULT token transfers to be unlocked after 30 minutes of the pool's launch (see [pool](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/d8b1c635c275d2a9450bd6a78f3fa2484fef73eb/contracts/UniswapV3Pool.sol#L276)). After this, the first swap will record an observation such that the initial liquidity reserves' price was maintained for the first 30 minutes ie. the full TWAP window. 

Add these lines to Whitelist.sol:setLocked() function, any buying transactions will revert in _beforeTokenTransfer => checkWhitelist() before at least 30 minutes have passed since pool initialization. 

```
require(_pool.observations[0].initialized, "Pool not initialized");
require(block.timestamp > _pool.observations[0].blockTimestamp + 30 minutes, "TWAP window has not passed");
```





## Assessed type

Oracle

# Vulnerability details

##Vulnerability Details
The `peek` function in the `UniswapV3Oracle` hard-codes a 5% slippage protection, which may not optimally adapt to various market conditions such as high volatility or liquidity imbalances.

## Impact
The primary concern is the potential for inaccuracies in price estimations due to the fixed 5% slippage protection, which could lead to for example reduced market efficiency.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L45

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There are 2 ways to mitigate this issue. First workaround is to implement a slippage protection that is set by the operator/manager of the contract and the second more preferable way is to allow users to determine the maximum slippage they are willing to take. Thic can be further implemented on the front-end.

The latter approach is the better choice since the market could change fast before the operator can apply the necessary slippage changes.


## Assessed type

Uniswap

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Uniswap's math libraries depend on wrapping behavior for arithmetic operations. However, Solidity version 0.8.0 introduced checked arithmetic by default, meaning that operations causing an overflow will revert. Since the original code was adapted from Uniswap and written in Solidity version 0.7.6, these arithmetic operations should be enclosed within an unchecked block to maintain the intended functionality. Considering the critical role that the FullMath and TickMath libraries play in calculating liquidity and pricing within the protocol I believe this should be a high. The functions - `getLiquidityForAmount0`, `getLiquidityForAmount1`, `getAmount0ForLiquidity`, and `getAmount1ForLiquidity` provided are fundamental to determining the value of liquidity positions and the amounts of tokens corresponding to those positions. If these calculations are incorrect due to unhandled overflows or underflows, it could lead to significant issues. Incorrect calculations in these areas can lead to mispricing of tokens, which could result in users receiving incorrect amounts of tokens upon trading or withdrawing liquidity. This could potentially lead to loss of funds for users or the protocol itself.

## Proof of Concept

The allowance approval in `Vultisig::approveAndCall()` is not set to zero initially which could potentially lead to issues when the contract interacts with non-standard ERC20 tokens such as USDT (Tether) for example, due to the nature & logic of that token. # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L62
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L39-L46
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L189


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The protocol using this oracle could face significant financial losses due to mispriced trades.

## Vulnerability Details

The combination of the `UniswapV3Oracle` contract and the `OracleLibrary` is crucial in determining price feeds based on Uniswap V3 Pool data. However, the reliance on certain Uniswap V3 pool mechanincs introduces potential vulnerabilities, particularly when it comes to the manipulation of `slot0` which is the most recent data point and can be manipulated easily via MEV bots and Flashloans with sandwich attacks.

The `UniswapV3Oracle` relies heavily on the state of `slot0` for its calculations as it contains critical data such as the current price, tick, and observation indices. Any manipulation of `slot0` directly affects the outputs of the oracle, leading to potential mispricing.

The function `getOldestObservationSEcondsAgo` determines how far back the oldest price observation was recorded. If an attacker can manipulate the pool to create misleading observations, this could affect the period calculation.

The `consult` function uses these observations to calculate a TWAP, which is supposed to smooth out short-term price volatility, however if observations have been manipulated, the TWAP itself becomse unreliable.

Aside from this, the `peek` function applies a static 5% slippage protection. This static value does not adapt to market conditions or levels of manipulation, making it potentially insufficient during high volatility or manipulation events.

## PoC

Consider the following scenario:

An attacker identifies the target Uniswap V3 pool (VULT/WETH) and the oracle using it
He takes out a large flash loan of VULT and/or WETH
Then he conducts large trades to manipulate the price in the VULT/WELTH pool, which directly affects the `slot0` data and the recorded observations. This will skew the dataset the oracle uses.
The `OracleLibrary.consult()` function retrieves the manipulated observations. The TWAP calculation is based on these skewed observations, resulting in an incorrect average price.
The `peek()` function applies a static 5% slippage, which may not cover the extend of manipulation. The attacker can then exploit the difference between the manipulated TWAP price and the actual market price. This would allow arbitrage opportunities from the discrepancy between the manipulated oracle price and other market prices.
Tha attacker then completes the trades to profit from these discrepancies, often completing the flash loan repayment and extracting the profit.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended mitigation steps

Implement a dynamic slippage mechanism that adjusts based on market conditions and detected volatility. Also consider using multiple data sources or oracles to cross-verify prices and reduce dependency on a single source.


## Assessed type

Oracle

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/base/LiquidityManagement.sol#L56


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `addLiquidity()` function in `LiquidityManagement` is trying to implement a price slippage check but it uses wrong logic which results in having no slippage check at all.

## Proof of Concept
The `amount0` and `amount1` returned from the uniswap pool `mint()` represent how much it costs to open a position with `params.liquidity`. To implement a slippage protection you need to have a value that represents the max that you are willing to give in order to provide this liquidity.
Currently it checks if `amount0`/`amount1` (the cost returned from uniswap) is gte
`params.amount0Min`/`params.amount1Min` (which is `totalRaised`).

Here is the require statement:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/base/LiquidityManagement.sol#L56
```solidity
require(amount0 >= params.amount0Min && amount1 >= params.amount1Min, "Price slippage check");
```
It checks if the `amount0` or `amount1` that represents the price that we are going to pay is gte our `totalRaise` token that we have, which does not make sense. We want to check if the `amount0` or `amount0` prices are in a range that we are willing to pay, not if they are gte the money that we have

## Tools Used
Manual Analysis
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To implement a correct price slippage check you need to create max variable which represent the maximum amount of tokens that you are willing to give for the `params.liquidity`


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/extensions/VultisigWhitelisted.sol#L22-L24
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L148-L150


# Vulnerability details

In `VultisigWhitelisted.sol`, the contract allows for the assignment of a whitelist contract. This whitelist contract not only assigns the `vultisig` token but also manages state, including blacklisted and whitelisted addresses. It is crucial for the code to ensure that the whitelist contract starts with an empty state and correctly assigns the `vultisig` token. To achieve this, executing both operations in a single atomic transaction is proposed to prevent any issues with stale or improperly initialized data.

## Impact

In the current implementation of `VultisigWhitelisted.sol`, there is a potential issue related to assigning a `whitelist` contract. Specifically:

1. **Token Assignment Consistency:** When assigning a new `whitelist` contract, it's crucial to ensure that the associated `vultisig` token is correctly assigned to this new contract instance. Failure to do so could lead to inconsistencies where the `vultisig` token does not correspond to the expected contract, potentially causing operational errors or security vulnerabilities.

2. **State Management of Whitelist Contract:** The `whitelist` contract can maintain state, such as blacklisted and whitelisted addresses. When assigning a new `whitelist` contract, it's essential to verify that this contract starts with a clean state. Failing to reset or clear the state could result in unintended access permissions or operational discrepancies.
## Proof of concept

#### First Problem Scenario:

When `VultisigWhitelisted` assigns a new `whitelist` contract:

- **Token Assignment Verification:** Ensure that the `vultisig` token assigned to the new `whitelist` contract is the correct one and matches expectations.
- **State Initialization:** Verify that the state of the new `whitelist` contract is empty or appropriately initialized to prevent stale or conflicting data from affecting operations.

#### Second Problem Scenario:

If an existing `Whitelist` is reassigned to a new `vultisig` token:

- **State Reset Requirement:** Prior to assigning the new `vultisig` token, ensure that the state of the existing `Whitelist` contract, including any blacklisted or whitelisted addresses, is reset or cleared. This prevents potential conflicts or unauthorized access due to outdated state information.

## Tools Used 

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps  

I'm suggesting to embed the whitelisting to the `VultisigWhitelisted` this will make the code more robust and will prevent from future problems. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

The `Whitelist::checkWhitelist` function has two significant issues. Firstly, it relies on the Uniswap oracle TWAP (time-weighted average price) to get the price, which can be manipulated. Secondly, the function allows users to bypass the `maxAddressCap` check if they use a small amount that results in `estimatedETHAmount` being zero, causing the cap check to always pass.

### Impact

1. **Price Manipulation via Uniswap Oracle TWAP:**

- Attackers can manipulate the TWAP by conducting large trades within a short time frame, influencing the reported price. This can lead to incorrect pricing, which may result in users being able to whitelist at unfavorable rates, causing financial loss or arbitrage opportunities. You should never relay on uniswap oracle price. It could lead to 
2. **Bypassing `maxAddressCap`:**

- Users can circumvent the `maxAddressCap` by using small amounts that result in `estimatedETHAmount` being zero. This means the check designed to limit the amount a single address can whitelist fails, allowing users to exceed the intended cap and potentially exploit the system for excessive allocation.

## Proof of concept

- **Price Manipulation:**

  An attacker can repeatedly trade a token pair on Uniswap within a short time window to skew the TWAP. For example, buying a large amount of ETH to spike the price and then selling it back can create an artificially high TWAP, which the `checkWhitelist` function uses, resulting in incorrect price calculations.
  
- **Bypassing `maxAddressCap`:**

  If `maxAddressCap` is set to a certain value and the user inputs a small amount that causes `estimatedETHAmount` to be zero, the check will pass everytime.

## Recommended mitigation steps

**Mitigate Price Manipulation:**

Use Chainlink Price Feeds as a reliable price oracle. Chainlink Price Feeds aggregate data from multiple sources and are resistant to manipulation.

**Prevent Bypassing `maxAddressCap`:**

Ensure that `estimatedETHAmount` accurately reflects small amounts and enforce a minimum amount requirement to prevent zero values.

```diff
uint256 estimatedETHAmount = IOracle(_oracle).peek(amount); // if peek result zero, this will
if (_contributed[to] + estimatedETHAmount > _maxAddressCap 
+ && estimatedETHAmount > 0 ) {
    revert MaxAddressCapOverflow();
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L213-L225
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L259-L261


# Vulnerability details

In the `claim` function, during fee calculation, there is a potential for overflow due to the way fees are computed based on the user's position. Specifically, the calculation can result in `amount0 + fees0 > amountCollected0`, causing an overflow. This issue arises because during the collect process, all fees collected up to that point, along with the burned amount, are gathered. If an overflow occurs, all the fees might be transferred to the fee taker, leading to unintended fund distribution.

## Impact

The overflow issue in the `claim` function can have several severe consequences:

1. **Unauthorized Fund Transfer:** If an overflow occurs, the fee taker might receive more fees than intended, including the entire amount collected so far.
2. **Financial Loss:** Other users could be deprived of their rightful fees, leading to significant financial losses.
3. **System Exploit:** Malicious users could exploit this vulnerability to drain funds from the contract, undermining the trust and stability of the system.
## Proof of Concept 

   Fees are calculated using the following formula:

```
uint256 fees0 = FullMath.mulDiv(feeGrowthInside0LastX128 - position.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,positionLiquidity,FixedPoint128.Q128 );
```
  
   After the calculation, it can happen that `amount0 + fees0 > amountCollected0`, leading to an overflow.
   
  **Simple example:** 
  A user initiates a claim and withdraws all fees and burned amount from the contract. If another user calls the claim function immediately after, the fee calculation could result in `fees0 + amount0` being higher than `amountCollected0`. The reason for this is that `position.feeGrowthInside0LastX128` (based on only one token) could have a very small value compared to the real `feeGrowthInside0LastX128` of the contract position. Since the contract version is below 0.8.0, this overflow will not revert the transaction, and the overflowed value will be treated as valid, leading to the unintended transfer of excess fees to the user.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps  

1. **Upgrade Solidity Version:**
  
   Upgrade the contract to Solidity version 0.8.0 or above to benefit from built-in overflow checks.
2. **Implement Overflow Checks:**

   Explicitly check for potential overflows in the fee calculation and handle them appropriately.

```solidity
require(amount0 + fees0 <= amountCollected0, "Overflow: fees exceed collected amount");
```

3. **Separate Fee Calculation and Collection:**
   
   Separate the fee calculation logic from the collection logic to ensure accurate tracking and prevent manipulation. This is the point that i suggest to separate the two.

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L204


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The `checkWhitelist` function in the `Whitelist` contract aims to enforce restrictions during the whitelist period. It checks if the sender (`from`) is the Uniswap V3 pool and the recipient (`to`) is not the owner. If these conditions are met, it proceeds to apply whitelist checks.

However, the check for the Uniswap V3 pool is flawed. It simply compares the sender's address to the stored `_pool` address. This is insufficient because the actual interaction with the pool occurs through the pool's contract, not directly from the pool's address.

As a result, anyone can bypass the whitelist check by directly interacting with the pool's contract to perform actions such as adding/removing liquidity or collecting fees. These actions are also subject to whitelist restrictions and should not be allowed during the whitelist period.

Furthermore, the exclusion of transactions where the recipient (`to`) is the owner could be exploited. If an attacker can manipulate the transaction to make it appear as if the owner is the recipient, they could bypass the whitelist entirely, regardless of the sender.

## Impact
This vulnerability allows attackers to bypass the whitelist restrictions and perform various actions on the Uniswap V3 pool during the whitelist period. This could lead to:

*   Unfair Token Distribution: Early buyers could acquire a disproportionate share of tokens through various pool interactions, potentially harming the project's tokenomics and community sentiment.
*   Market Manipulation: The unrestricted pool interactions could lead to artificial price manipulation, creating a false sense of demand and potentially misleading other investors.
*   Financial Losses: If the project relies on the whitelist to raise funds or control initial token distribution, this vulnerability could undermine those goals and lead to financial losses.

## Proof of Concept
1.  **Setup:**
    *   Deploy the `VultisigWhitelisted`, `Whitelist`, and `UniswapV3Oracle` contracts.
    *   Set up a Uniswap V3 pool for the VULT/ETH pair.
    *   Configure the `Whitelist` contract with the correct pool and oracle addresses.
    *   Add some initial liquidity to the pool.

2.  **Attacker Interaction:**
    *   The attacker interacts directly with the pool's contract to perform actions such as:
        *   Swapping ETH for VULT tokens using `swapExactInputSingle`.
        *   Adding liquidity to the pool using `mint`.
        *   Removing liquidity from the pool using `burn`.
        *   Collecting fees from the pool using `collect`.
    *   Since the attacker is interacting directly with the pool contract, the `checkWhitelist` function in the `Whitelist` contract is not triggered, or is bypassed due to the owner exclusion.
    *   The attacker successfully performs these actions without any whitelist restrictions.

3.  **Verification:**
    *   Check the attacker's VULT token balance and ETH balance. They should have changed according to the actions performed.
    *   Check the pool's liquidity and fee statistics. They should also reflect the attacker's actions.

This PoC demonstrates how the incorrect check for Uniswap V3 pool interactions and the potential owner manipulation allow attackers to bypass the whitelist and perform various actions on the pool freely.

## Tools Used
Hardhat

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1.  **Correct Pool Interaction Check:** Modify the `checkWhitelist` function to correctly identify interactions originating from the Uniswap V3 pool contract. This could involve checking the calldata or using a more robust method to verify the interaction source.
2.  **Remove or Secure Owner Exclusion:** Consider removing the exclusion for transactions where the recipient is the owner. If this exclusion is necessary, implement additional checks to ensure that the owner is not being impersonated or manipulated into participating in malicious transactions.
3.  **Implement Additional Whitelist Checks:** Explore adding more comprehensive whitelist checks for all relevant pool interactions, including adding/removing liquidity and collecting fees. This would ensure that all actions are restricted during the whitelist period, preventing any potential bypasses.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L221


# Vulnerability details

#### Vulnerability Details

**Summary:**
A critical vulnerability in the `Whitelist` contract allows attackers to bypass the maximum ETH contribution limit by exploiting the incorrect estimation of the ETH equivalent of VULT tokens.

**Affected Contracts:**
- `Whitelist.sol`
- `oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol`

**Root Cause:**
The `checkWhitelist` function estimates the ETH equivalent of VULT tokens using the `peek` function from the `UniswapV3Oracle` contract. The slippage is incorrectly applied as a discount instead of a premium, leading to an underestimated ETH amount.

**Affected Code:**
In `Whitelist.sol`:
```solidity
uint256 estimatedETHAmount = IOracle(_oracle).peek(amount);
if (_contributed[to] + estimatedETHAmount > _maxAddressCap) {
    revert MaxAddressCapOverflow();
}
_contributed[to] += estimatedETHAmount;
```

In `UniswapV3Oracle.sol`:
```solidity
uint256 quotedWETHAmount = OracleLibrary.getQuoteAtTick(tick, BASE_AMOUNT, baseToken, WETH);
return (quotedWETHAmount * baseAmount * 95) / 1e20; // Incorrect slippage applied
```

**Impact:**
An attacker can exploit this to contribute more ETH than the allowed cap, acquiring a larger share of tokens than intended. This leads to financial losses for the project and genuine contributors, and damages the project's reputation.

**Proof of Concept:**
1. An attacker prepares to purchase VULT tokens, aware of the incorrect slippage calculation.
2. The attacker initiates a transaction to buy VULT tokens, exceeding the maximum ETH cap.
3. The `checkWhitelist` function calls the `peek` function, which underestimates the ETH amount.
4. The underestimated ETH amount allows the transaction to pass, bypassing the cap.

#### Tools Used
Manual code review and analysis

#### Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Correct the slippage calculation in the `peek` function of the `UniswapV3Oracle` contract to:
```solidity
return (quotedWETHAmount * baseAmount * 105) / 1e20; // Correctly applying 5% slippage
```
2. Conduct a comprehensive review of all mathematical calculations in the `Whitelist` and `UniswapV3Oracle` contracts to ensure no other similar errors exist.


## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In ILOManager.sol can be found initILOPool() that can be called from onlyProjectAdmin. This function is responsible for initialization of pools. We can see that there is a require that says ``` require(sqrtRatioLowerX96 < _project.initialPoolPriceX96 && sqrtRatioLowerX96 < sqrtRatioUpperX96, "RANGE"); ``` .This require can be bypassed by a pool which initial price is far more bigger than the lower tick and higher tick. In this case the pool will be invalid. As an impact since the price is outside the tick range, there will be no active liquidity available at the current price. This means that any swap attempts at this price will fail as there is no liquidity for the trade. Also the mentioned invariant from the sponsor: ``Once project inits, it inits a uniswap v3 pool. That pool address will be used as project id. You cannot change initial price after project is initialized``- means that liquidity will be temporary locked until the price goes to the expected tick ratio.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L90

Initial price=5
tickLower=1
tickUpper=3

In this case with the current implementation an invalid pool will be initialized.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the require in order to not make it impossible to initialize invalid pool. For example:
```
require (sqrtRatioLowerX96 < _project.initialPoolPriceX96 && _project.initialPoolPriceX96 < sqrtRatioUpperX96 &&
 sqrtRatioLowerX96 < sqrtRatioUpperX96, "RANGE");
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L79-L84


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol deploys ILOPool(s) using the cloneDeterministic method from OpenZeppelin's Clones library, which uses the CREATE2 opcode. The deployment process is as follows:

```js
    bytes32 salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(
        ChainId.get(),
        params.uniV3Pool,
        _initializedILOPools[params.uniV3Pool].length
    ));
    iloPoolAddress = Clones.cloneDeterministic(ILO_POOL_IMPLEMENTATION, salt);
```
Out of these three values used to compute the salt, `params.uniV3Pool` is known to any user monitoring the mempool as soon as the transaction is broadcasted. 

Furthermore, since the protocol only intends to deploy on Ethereum mainnet, the `chainId` is always fixed to `1`.

The `_initializedILOPools[params.uniV3Pool].length` is only updated after a successful `ILOManager::initPool` call. Since for the first ILOPool deployment for a particular `params.uniV3Pool`, the length is `0`, making the salt predictable.

For the master, `ILO_POOL_IMPLEMENTATION` is used, which is a public variable. 

This allows a malicious actor to deploy a contract with the same master and salt before the protocol does, making every call to `ILOManager::initPool` revert as there is already a contract at the address that create2 tries to deploys to.

This can be done repeatedly resulting in a DoS for `ILOManager::initPool`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the salt generation mechanism to include a random nonce.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/libraries/LiquidityAmounts.sol#L10


# Vulnerability details

The `LiquidityAmounts` library implements the liquidity amount functions for computing liquidity amounts from token amounts and prices. However , it does not implements the `getLiquidityForAmounts` and `getAmountsForLiquidity` functions.

## Impact
The protocol could require these functions.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/ILOManager.sol#L58


# Vulnerability details

The `claimRefund` function allows users to refund their bought raised tokens. This function can only be called after the refund deadline has passed.

```javascript
require(block.timestamp >= _project.refundDeadline, "RFT");
```

However, once the launch is triggered, the `claimRefund` function is no longer available. During the `initProject`, we ensure that the `refundDeadline` is set appropriately.

```javascript
 function initProject(InitProjectParams calldata params) external override afterInitialize() returns(address   uniV3PoolAddress) {
@>      uint64 refundDeadline = params.launchTime + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_OFFSET;

        PoolAddress.PoolKey memory poolKey = PoolAddress.getPoolKey(params.saleToken, params.raiseToken, params.fee);
        uniV3PoolAddress = _initUniV3PoolIfNecessary(poolKey, params.initialPoolPriceX96);
        
        _cacheProject(uniV3PoolAddress, params.saleToken, params.raiseToken, params.fee, params.initialPoolPriceX96, params.launchTime, refundDeadline);
        emit ProjectCreated(uniV3PoolAddress, _cachedProject[uniV3PoolAddress]);
    }
```
So the problem is with the `params.launchTime`, which is the designated launch time for any project. Additionally, we add the `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_OFFSET` to the `refundDeadline`. This setup implies that the project will `launch` at that `launchTime` in the ILOPool.sol contract. Since we cannot `claimRefund` before the assigned deadline, we must wait until the `launchTime + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_OFFSET`. However, during this period, the `launch` would have already been triggered in the `ILOPool.sol` contract, and due to this `launch` being triggered, we will not be able to `claimRefund`.

## Impact
User will not able to `claimRefund` anymore.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/ILOManager.sol#L58

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/ILOManager.sol#L144

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src/ILOPool.sol#L342

```javascript
 uint64 refundDeadline = params.launchTime + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_OFFSET;
```
`refundDeadline` is after `launchTime` , but since the project will be launch at that `launchTime`, we wil not able to `claimRefund` anymore.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider don't assigning `refundDeadline` with `launchTime` would be the great solution here.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `initialize` function in the contract `ILOPool` can be called by any account, not necessarily just the contract owner or manager. This represents a security issue as this function sets the initial parameters of the pool which should be a privileged functionality usually limited to contract creators or administrators.

This lack of access control mechanism could allow any attacker to set malicious values by calling the `initialize` method.


## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function initialize(InitPoolParams calldata params) external override whenNotInitialized() {
    ...
}

## Tools Used

manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this vulnerability, restrict the access to the `initialize` function. This can be done by adding an access control rule — if there is a specific owner or privileged role who should have access to this function. It is possible to integrate OpenZeppelin's `Ownable` or `AccessControl` libraries for managing roles and privileges. Implementing the changes would look like the following:

```solidity
function initialize(InitPoolParams calldata params) external override onlyOwner {
    ...
}
```

This will ensure that only the owner of the contract can call the `initialize` function. The `onlyOwner` function modifier is a part of OpenZeppelin's Ownable library and it automatically reverts any transaction from accounts that are not the owner.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

In the `ILOManager.sol:initILOPool` function there are no checks to ensure that the 
Project have not been launched before adding a new pool to the pool array, So pools can be added even after the project is launched.

The `ILOManager.sol:launch` function loops through the `initializedPools` array and launches each pool individually.

The problem is that the `IILOPool(initializedPools[i]).launch();` function reverts if the pool has already been launched. So the pools added after launch cannot be launched.

```solidity
    function launch(address uniV3PoolAddress) external override {
        ...
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < initializedPools.length; i++) {
@->         IILOPool(initializedPools[i]).launch();
        }

        emit ProjectLaunch(uniV3PoolAddress);
    }

```



## Impact

The pool cannot be launched, and funds are lost.

## Proof of Concept


## Tools Used

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Prevent pools from being added after project has been launched

DoS

 function addLiquidity(AddLiquidityParams memory params)
        internal
        returns (
            uint256 amount0,
            uint256 amount1
        )
    {
        (amount0, amount1) = params.pool.mint(
            address(this),
            TICK_LOWER,
            TICK_UPPER,
            params.liquidity,
            ""
        );

        require(amount0 >= params.amount0Min && amount1 >= params.amount1Min, 'Price slippage check');
    }
```
This is somewhat similar to how liquidty is added to a position in uniswap v2
https://github.com/Uniswap/v2-periphery/blob/0335e8f7e1bd1e8d8329fd300aea2ef2f36dd19f/contracts/UniswapV2Router02.sol#L61
This is the deadline check used univ2
```
modifier ensure(uint deadline) {
    require(deadline >= block.timestamp, 'UniswapV2Router: EXPIRED');
    _;
}
```
This deadline check ensure that the transaction can be executed on time and the expired transaction revert.

## Tools Used
Code Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a similar check like this of uniswapv2
```
modifier ensure(uint deadline) {
    require(deadline >= block.timestamp, 'UniswapV2Router: EXPIRED');
    _;
}
```





## Assessed type

Uniswap

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/TickMath.sol#L1-L2
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L1-L2
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L1-L2


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `TickMath` library was adjusted to allow compilations for solidity version 0.8. This library relies on implicit overflow behavior to function correctly. The issue is that the contract `UniswapV3Oracle` is compiled with solidity 0.8 and indirectly uses the `TickMath` library via the `OracleLibrary`. Since this contract will be compiled with solidity 0.8, it could in the worst case scenario, make the library `TickMath` revert instead of implicitely overflowing as in the previous versions. This will lead to a revert in the `UniswapV3Oracle::peek` function which in turn will cause the `Whitelist::checkWhitelist` to revert.

## Proof of Concept
The `pragma solidity >=0.5.0;` instead of `pragma solidity >=0.5.0 <0.8.0;` adjustment has been made for the `TickMath` library :
```js
// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
pragma solidity >=0.5.0;
```

This allows it to be compiled with solidity 0.8 when the contract `UniswapV3Oracle` is compiled. This negates any overflow behavior in the library `TickMath` which by default relies on.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using the [TickMath 0.8 official version](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/0.8/contracts/libraries/TickMath.sol#L27) which uses `unchecked` blocks for every function. Consider using  two different versions of this file, one for solidity versions <0.8 and one for 0.8 from the 0.8 branch.


## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`ILOPool` is an `ERC721` token that can be traded freely on the secondary markets (example Opensea). These NFTs are tied to vesting balances in the `ILOPool` contract. Since the owner of the nft can call the `ILOPool::claim()` to claim his vested amount at any moment (after launch), it exposes buyers of NFTs on secondary markets to the risk of acquiring devalued assets.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario :

- Alice mints an NFT tied to a vested position in the pool after calling `buy` function.
- Alice decides to sell the NFT on a secondary market like OpenSea after discussing the terms with a buyer.
- Prior to the sale, Alice claims the accrued vested tokens associated with the NFT, significantly reducing the value tied to the NFT.
- At the same time the buyer sends buying TX and receives the NFT with much less vested amounts than he expected, overpaying for the the asset.
## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding functionality that pauses claims or refunds when the NFT is for sale.


## Assessed type

ERC721

# Vulnerability details

## Description
In the readme, its mentioned: Anyone can launch the pool when all conditions met.
Consider these possible scenarios:

- A denial of service attack on the blockchain has prevented transactions occurring for a significant period of time.
- An extreme spike in gas prices has prevented transactions occurring for a significant period of time.
- Some unforeseen technical error takes the blockchain down, perhaps during an upgrade or fork.

Now due to any of the above scenarios the [oldest observation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L39) is more than 30 minutes due to which default [PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L41) will be used to get TWAT(time-weighted average tick).
These 30 minutes give a perfect time window for a malicious act to be perform as you can see here in the [chart](https://x.com/bantg/status/1455151835828867079) a moment where DUCK/WETH@1% went to zero in a 30min TWAT oracle
## Impact
Malicious actors could use the current [PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L16) time window to swap at an inflation rate
## Proof of Concept
If, due to any scenario, the next call to observation is after 30 minutes, the attacker could use this timeframe window and just after 30 minutes tick calculated value, swap the affected tokens at a high inflation rate.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The advice would be to increase the period time to make sure the protocol oracle is more secure in high volatility time or calculate avg observations time and if the obs value is above this simply reject it or put a warning flag








## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L16


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Update periods in TWAP oracles reflect risk of an asset. Updating more frequently accurately prices an asset but increases capabilities of manipulation (which should be harder with more stable assets), whereas longer update periods prevent manipulation but does not accurately price assets (due to the time difference between updates). Volatility of an asset should be considered when calculating update periods. However, in Vultsig's UniswapV3Oracle.sol no such considerations are made, the [PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L16) cannot be changed after deployment of the contract. Additionally, each asset uses the same PERIOD which does not adequately account for the differences in risk for each asset. This could lead to price manipulation or inadequate pricing of assets.
## Proof of Concept
[PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L16) will be set to 30 minutes during the deployment.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Either add an `onlyOwner` function to update the period or simply generate a warning flag whenever a pool is prone to any issues related to assets pricing.


## Assessed type

Timing

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/FullMath.sol#L14
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/FullMath.sol#L109
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/TickMath.sol#L23
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/TickMath.sol#L61


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Uniswap math libraries rely on wrapping behavior for conducting arithmetic operations. Solidity
version 0.8.0 introduced checked arithmetic by default where operations that cause an overflow would revert.
Since the code was adapted from Uniswap these arithmetic operations should be wrapped in an unchecked block.
As the present spdx version of fullMath.sol and tickmath.sol is [>=0.4.0](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/FullMath.sol#L2)&[>=0.5.0](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/TickMath.sol#L2C17-L2C24)
due to this any call that leads to overflow, underflow will be reverted.
This happens because from solidity version 0.8.0 checked is by default as mentioned in their [docs](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/control-structures.html#checked-or-unchecked-arithmetic)
>As impacts would be too many I am here talking about one of them.

**Impact:**
Due to [_saleAmountNeeded](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L382) using getLiquidityForAmount1, getLiquidityForAmount0, etc which uses FullMath.sol for calculations, sale token amount needed for the raise Amount will be far off what actually it should be.
## Proof of Concept
The Uniswap protocol has a reference implementation for these changes in a branch named [0.8.](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/tree/0.8)
Here are correct version of [TickMath.sol](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/0.8/contracts/libraries/TickMath.sol) and [FullMath.sol](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/0.8/contracts/libraries/FullMath.sol)
This was also reported by [Pashov](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-01-tickmath-and-fullmath-libraries-are-missing-unchecked-pashov-none-tapiocadao-markdown),[spearbit](https://solodit.xyz/issues/use-unchecked-intickmathsol-andfullmathsol-spearbit-overlay-pdf)



## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the official [Uniswapv0.8](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/tree/0.8) library.


























## Assessed type

Library

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
As the current version of OracleLibrary.sol is [>=0.5.0](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L2) due to which any call that could lead to overflow and underflow will get reverted.
This happens because in solidity 0.8.0 checked is by default as mentioned in their [docs](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/control-structures.html#checked-or-unchecked-arithmetic)
This happens due to not implementing an unchecked block [OracleLibrary.sol#consult](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L14) could give a wrong value.
## Proof of Concept
**Scenario: Overflow**
- [tickCumulativesDelta](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L22): -1 (Assuming a negative delta for this example)
- period: block.timestamp (Positive integer)
Here's why overflow can occur
The calculation would be int24(-1 / block.timestamp). This results in a negative int24 value (let's say x).
The if statement checks if tickCumulativesDelta (which is 1 in this case) is negative and has a non-zero remainder after dividing by period. Since block.timestamp is positive, there will always be a remainder.
Due to the negative bias, the code attempts to decrement timeWeightedAverageTick (which has the value x from the calculation).
If -x is the minimum representable value for int24 (negative 2^23), decrementing it will cause an overflow and wrap around to the maximum positive value (2^23 - 1).

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the version to 0.8.0 and use unchecked block




















## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

**Root cause:**
According to the [documentation](https://docs.vultisig.com/vultisig-token/usdvltx), the Vultisig token is expected to be Burnable. This is not true currently since the  internal ERC20 _burn() function is not exposed externally through another wrapped external/public function. 

**Impact:**
According to the [documentation](https://docs.vultisig.com/vultisig-token/usdvltx#value-accrual), the token is expected to have a "Value Accrual" model in the Vultisig system, which as stated is termed as the buy-burn model. 

From the docs:
```
All affiliate, router, and bridge fees accumulated from platform usage will be used to buy and burn the asset.

Through the buy and burn-burn model, the token automatically increases in value the more the app is used to swap and bridge.
```

As we can see, due to the missing burn functionality, the Vultisig token would fail to increase in value due to the supply not decreasing. This hampers the economic model/value of the token and fails to meet its expected value accrual design in the ecosystem.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Expose the internal _burn() function using a wrapper external/public function. Ensure that the msg.sender can burn his tokens only.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Vultisig.sol#L18


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

**Context:**
Function [approveAndCall()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Vultisig.sol#L16) is used to approve vultisig tokens to a spender and make an external call to function receiveApproval() on the spender contract, which uses transferFrom() to spend the allowance provided.

**Root cause:**
In the function approveAndCall() though, the internal function _approve() [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Vultisig.sol#L18) and the external call [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Vultisig.sol#L21) are called with msg.sender instead of using _msgSender() from the Context.sol library inherited by the ERC20 token contract.

**Impact:**
This is being reported as a Medium-severity risk issue since all user facing public functions in the ERC20 token contract i.e. [transfer()](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/442886ed5ff8a0b9ab477b191f5238541ee6d772/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol#L104), [transferFrom()](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/442886ed5ff8a0b9ab477b191f5238541ee6d772/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol#L149) and even [approve()](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/442886ed5ff8a0b9ab477b191f5238541ee6d772/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol#L127) itself uses _msgSender() to retrieve data about the sender of the transaction. When dealing with meta-transactions, the account sending and paying for execution may not be the actual sender but might be some sort of GSN ([1](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/v3.4.0/contracts/GSN/GSNRecipient.sol#L90), [2](https://opengsn.org/)).

This can break the composability with external applications that use approveAndCall() to approve + transfer at the same time to save gas for the trusted spender contract. 

## Proof of Concept

In the Vultisig contract below, we can see that Line 21 and Line 25 directly use msg.sender instead of _msgSender(). As stated above, this can prevent applications from composing and using this specific functionality of the token.
```solidity
File: Vultisig.sol
18:     function approveAndCall(address spender, uint256 amount, bytes calldata extraData) external returns (bool) {
19:         // Approve the spender to spend the tokens
20:         
21:         _approve(msg.sender, spender, amount);
22: 
23:         // Call the receiveApproval function on the spender contract
24:         
25:         IApproveAndCallReceiver(spender).receiveApproval(msg.sender, amount, address(this), extraData);
26: 
27:         return true;
28:     }
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace both msg.sender instances with _msgSender().


## Assessed type

Context

This checks if a pool exists or not. If it does not, it creates a pool and initializes it. If it does, it ensures a price is initialized or the current price meets the existing price retrieved from slot0. 

**Root cause:**
The issue will be described in the POC but the root cause is the missing 0 value check for sqrtPriceX96 in the if condition [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L111).

**Impact:**
The impact of this issue would be that the admin of the project will not be able to set an initial price for pool (project) anymore or the prices would mismatch if initialized directly through the pool.

The issue is presented in a specific scenario.

It is possible for an investor to have two NFT tokenIds if someone sold their position or whitelist spot to them. But the current implementation, hardcodes 0 when retrieving the tokenId for the investor through tokenOfOwnerByIndex [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L147). 

This forces the investor to only be able to use their first tokenId instead of the second one they received. 

## Proof of Concept

1. Investor B provides A with their tokenId by transferring it.

2. Investor A decides to add liquidity to the tokenId they just received using the [buy()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOPool.sol#L126) function. But since A cannot pass in index 1 (representing the 2nd tokenId they have) as a parameter, they are forced to use the first ID at index0.

134:         returns (
135:             uint256 tokenId,
136:             uint128 liquidityDelta
137:         )
138:     { 
```

We can see that only index 0 is considered on Line 155 which represents the A's first tokenId.
```solidity

150:         if (balanceOf(recipient) == 0) {
151:             _mint(recipient, (tokenId = _nextId++));
152:             _positionVests[tokenId].schedule = _vestingConfigs[0].schedule;
153:         } else {
154:              
155:             tokenId = tokenOfOwnerByIndex(recipient, 0);

```

Allow investor to supply which NFT tokenId they want to add liquidity to through the buy() function.

## Impact
Someone can effectively DoS every project launch.

## Proof of Concept
We have this validation:

    require(_cachedProject[uniV3PoolAddress].initialPoolPriceX96 == sqrtPriceX96, "UV3P");

[Line#190](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L190)

One approach I could think of is refactoring the logic so the UniswapV3 pool is created with the launch.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L29-L31


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Using tx.origin can lead to an unintended party gaining control of the contract. This happens because tx.origin refers to the original sender of the transaction, which can be different from msg.sender if the transaction is relayed through another contract. As a result, the contract might mistakenly assign ownership to an intermediary contract instead of the actual deployer.

## Proof of Concept
Original Constructor (Vulnerable):

constructor() {
    transferOwnership(tx.origin);
}

Explanation:
In this version, the ownership is transferred to tx.origin. If the contract deployment is proxied or relayed through another contract, tx.origin will point to the address that initially initiated the transaction, which might not be the intended owner.

Exploiting the Vulnerability:

An attacker deploys a relay contract.
The attacker uses this relay contract to deploy the ILOManager contract.
The tx.origin points to the attacker's address, not the actual deployer's address.
The attacker gains ownership of the ILOManager contract.
In this scenario, the owner of ILOManager becomes the attacker because tx.origin refers to the attacker's address who initiated the transaction through the Relay contract.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this, use msg.sender instead of tx.origin in the constructor to ensure the correct owner is set. msg.sender accurately represents the address that directly interacts with the contract.

constructor() {
    transferOwnership(msg.sender);
}

In the secure version, msg.sender is used to transfer ownership. This ensures that the ownership is correctly assigned to the address that directly interacts with the contract. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L39-L46


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The [UniswapV3Oracle.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L14) is compiled with version `0.8` and indirectly uses these libraries through the [OracleLibrary](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L9), which is compiled with `>=0.5.0`. In the worst case, it could be that the libraries always revert (instead of overflowing as in previous versions), leading to a broken `UniswapV3Oracle` contract.

## Proof of Concept
UniswapV3’s both `TickMath` and `FullMath` libraries was changed to allow compilations for solidity version 0.8. However, adjustments to account for the implicit overflow behavior that the contract relies upon were not performed.The [UniswapV3Oracle.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L14) is compiled with version [0.8](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L2) and indirectly uses these libraries through the [OracleLibrary](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L9) in [peek](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/UniswapV3Oracle.sol#L39-L46) function which returns the TWAP price for 1 VULT for the last 30 mins.
```solidity
   function peek(uint256 baseAmount) external view returns (uint256) {
        uint32 longestPeriod = OracleLibrary.getOldestObservationSecondsAgo(pool);
        uint32 period = PERIOD < longestPeriod ? PERIOD : longestPeriod;
        int24 tick = OracleLibrary.consult(pool, period);
        uint256 quotedWETHAmount = OracleLibrary.getQuoteAtTick(tick, BASE_AMOUNT, baseToken, WETH);
        // Apply 5% slippage
        return (quotedWETHAmount * baseAmount * 95) / 1e20; // 100 / 1e18
    }
```
The same pragma solidity `>=0.5.0` instead of pragma solidity `>=0.5.0 <0.8.0` adjustments have been made for the [OracleLibrary](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/oracles/uniswap/uniswapv0.8/OracleLibrary.sol#L2). However, their code does not rely on implicit overflow behavior. In the worst case, it could be that the libraries always revert (instead of overflowing as in previous versions), leading to a broken `UniswapV3Oracle` contract.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Follow the implementation of the official [TickMath](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/6562c52e8f75f0c10f9deaf44861847585fc8129/contracts/libraries/TickMath.sol#L7)/[FullMath](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/6562c52e8f75f0c10f9deaf44861847585fc8129/contracts/libraries/FullMath.sol#L7) 0.8 branch which uses `unchecked` blocks for every function. Consider using the official Uniswap files with two different versions of this file, one for solidity versions <0.8 and one for 0.8 from the 0.8 branch





## Assessed type

Library

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `claimProjectRefund` function uses the `OnlyManager` modifier instead of the `onlyProjectAdmin` modifier. According to the documentation, only the project admin should be able to initialize the ILO pool for the project and claim project refunds.

The current implementation violates the specified access control requirements by allowing the manager, instead of the project admin, to claim project refunds. This can lead to unauthorized access and potential misuse of the funds intended to be controlled by the project admin.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/src/ILOManager.sol#L201

Documentation:
Only project admin can init ILO pool for project `and claim project refund (sale token deposited into ILO pool).`



## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Replace the `OnlyManager` modifier with the `onlyProjectAdmin` modifier in the `claimProjectRefund` function to ensure that only the project admin can call this function.

```solidity
function claimProjectRefund(address projectAdmin) external override refundable() onlyProjectAdmin returns (uint256 refundAmount) {
    return _refundProject(projectAdmin);
}
```

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L65-L74


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `Whitelist` contract allows users to self-whitelist by sending ETH to the contract. If the self-whitelist feature is enabled, the contract sends back the received ETH to the sender using the low-level `transfer()` function. 

However, from [solidity docs](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.25/contracts.html#receive-ether-function),`transfer()` only forwards 2300 gas, which is insufficient for the recipient to execute any non-trivial logic in a `receive()` or `fallback` function. This can lead to a situation where the ETH transfer fails if the recipient is a contract that requires more than 2300 gas to process the transfer. As a result, the ETH could be locked in the `Whitelist` contract indefinitely, leading to a potential loss of funds for users who interact with the contract via multisig wallets or other smart contracts.

From the solidity docs:
>In the worst case, the receive function can only rely on 2300 gas being available (for example when send or transfer is used), leaving little room to perform other operations except basic logging. The following operations will consume more gas than the 2300 gas stipend:
>- Writing to storage
>- Creating a contract
>- Calling an external function which consumes a large amount of gas
>- Sending Ether


Also worthy to note that a similar bug was reported in the just concluded `Renzo` contest as seen here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo-findings/issues/612

## Proof of Concept
The `Whitelist` contract includes a `receive()` function that handles ETH transfers for self-whitelisting: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/cb72b1e9053c02a58d874ff376359a83dc3f0742/hardhat-vultisig/contracts/Whitelist.sol#L65-L74

```solidity
receive() external payable {
    if (_isSelfWhitelistDisabled) {
        revert SelfWhitelistDisabled();
    }
    if (_isBlacklisted[_msgSender()]) {
        revert Blacklisted();
    }
    _addWhitelistedAddress(_msgSender());
    payable(_msgSender()).transfer(msg.value);
}
```

In this function, the contract sends back the received ETH to the sender using `transfer()`. However, `transfer()` only forwards 2300 gas, which is not enough for the recipient to execute any non-trivial logic in a `receive()` or `fallback` function. For instance, multisig wallets or other smart contracts that have a `receive()` function requiring more than 2300 gas will fail to receive the ETH, causing the transaction to revert.

To summarise:
1. **Self-Whitelist Process**: Users can self-whitelist by sending ETH to the `Whitelist` contract. The contract checks if self-whitelisting is enabled and if the sender is not blacklisted. If these conditions are met, the sender is added to the whitelist, and the received ETH is sent back to the sender.

2. **Gas Limitation with `transfer()`**: The `transfer()` function only forwards 2300 gas, which is sufficient for simple transfers but not for contracts that require more gas to execute their `receive()` or `fallback` functions. This limitation can cause the ETH transfer to fail if the recipient is a contract that needs more gas.

3. **Impact on Multisig Wallets and Smart Contracts**: If a user interacts with the `Whitelist` contract using a multisig wallet or another smart contract that has a `receive()` function requiring more than 2300 gas, the ETH transfer will fail. This will cause the transaction to revert, and the ETH will remain locked in the `Whitelist` contract.

4. **Permanent Lockup of Funds**: Since the `receive()` function uses `transfer()`, any failed transfer due to gas limitations will result in the ETH being locked in the contract. Users who interact with the contract via multisig wallets or other smart contracts will be unable to retrieve their ETH, leading to a potential loss of funds.

Let's consider a scenario:
1. Alice uses a multisig wallet contract to send 1 ETH to the `Whitelist` contract to self-whitelist.
2. The multisig wallet contract is the `msg.sender` and gets saved as the whitelisted address.
3. The `Whitelist` contract attempts to send back the 1 ETH to the multisig wallet using `transfer()`.
4. The multisig wallet has a `receive()` function that requires more than 2300 gas to execute.
5. The `transfer()` function fails due to insufficient gas, causing the transaction to revert.
6. The 1 ETH is now locked in the `Whitelist` contract, and Alice cannot retrieve it.

## Tools used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
So as to avoid potential lockup of ETH in the `Whitelist` contract, replace the use of `transfer()` with `call()`. The `call()` function forwards all available gas, allowing the recipient contract to execute arbitrary logic in its `receive()` function. 


## Assessed type

ETH-Transfer

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

When a user claims their fees from `ILOPool.claim`, they receive their accrued fees up to that point. However, the function then attempts to send the `performance fee` to `feeTaker`, performing a collect on the Uniswap position with the amount `type(uint128).max`, which withdraws all fees from all users. This excess is then sent to feeTaker, causing potential DoS and future payment issues.

## Proof of Concept

ILOPool.sol:

```
(uint128 amountCollected0, uint128 amountCollected1) = pool.collect(
            address(this),
            TICK_LOWER,
            TICK_UPPER,
            type(uint128).max,
            type(uint128).max
        );

...

        address feeTaker = IILOManager(MANAGER).FEE_TAKER();
        // transfer fee to fee taker
        TransferHelper.safeTransfer(_cachedPoolKey.token0, feeTaker, amountCollected0-amount0);
        TransferHelper.safeTransfer(_cachedPoolKey.token1, feeTaker, amountCollected1-amount1);
```

amountCollected{0,1} represent the accumulated fees from all users, so feeTaker is receiving almost all the benefits.

## Tools Used

Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The function should send to feeTaker only the fees obtained relative to what the user claimed.

Uniswap

`require(block.timestamp > saleInfo.start && block.timestamp < saleInfo.end, "ST");`

## Summary
## Summary
The vulnerability in the Uniswap math libraries (`FullMath`, `Oraclelibrary` and `TickMath`) stems from the absence of the unchecked modifier in Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0. This oversight would lead to unintended reverts, affecting critical functionalities such as token swaps and liquidity management in UniswapV3.
## Impact
The absence of the `unchecked` modifier in these libraries could inadvertently cause transactions to revert when performing arithmetic operations that result in an overflow, despite the libraries' intention to handle "phantom overflow". This exist in the libraries `fullmath`, `oraclelibrary` and `tickmath` and will break the functionalities of the vultisig contracts dépending on them.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOManager.sol#L150
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOManager.sol#L155


# Vulnerability details

The owner can  set platform and performance fees to any value without any validation. Specifically, the functions `setPlatformFee` and `setPerformanceFee` can set `PLATFORM_FEE` and `PERFORMANCE_FEE` to any value, including unreasonably high values such as 100% or more. This lack of validation could lead to severe financial impacts on users.

## Impact

If the fees are set to excessively high values:
- Users could lose all their generated profits or even a significant portion of their principal.
- High or unpredictable fees would deter users from using the platform, impacting its adoption and liquidity.

## Proof of Concept

The following setter functions for platform and performance fees:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOManager.sol#L150
```solidity
function setPlatformFee(uint16 _platformFee) external onlyOwner {
    PLATFORM_FEE = _platformFee;
}
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOManager.sol#L155
```solidity
function setPerformanceFee(uint16 _performanceFee) external onlyOwner {
    PERFORMANCE_FEE = _performanceFee;
}
```

There is no validation to ensure that `_platformFee` and `_performanceFee` are within reasonable bounds.


The `_deductFees` function is used to deduct fees based on the provided `feeBPS` (basis points):
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOPool.sol#L438
```solidity
function _deductFees(uint256 amount0, uint256 amount1, uint16 feeBPS) internal pure 
    returns (uint256 amount0Left, uint256 amount1Left) {
    amount0Left = amount0 - FullMath.mulDiv(amount0, feeBPS, BPS);
    amount1Left = amount1 - FullMath.mulDiv(amount1, feeBPS, BPS);
}
```

When `feeBPS` is set to an excessively high value, such as 10000 (representing 100%), it results in:

```solidity
amount0Left = amount0 - FullMath.mulDiv(amount0, 10000, 10000); // amount0Left = amount0 - amount0 = 0
amount1Left = amount1 - FullMath.mulDiv(amount1, 10000, 10000); // amount1Left = amount1 - amount1 = 0
```

This means that after the deduction, `amount0Left` and `amount1Left` will both be 0. Consequently, the investor will receive no generated fees (profits).


Assume an investor's position has generated fees `fees0 = 100` and `fees1 = 50`:

- With `performanceFee = 10000` (100%):
  ```solidity
  (fees0, fees1) = _deductFees(100, 50, 10000); // results in (0, 0)
  ```

So, the investor would receive 0 for both `fees0` and `fees1`.


In the `claim` function, this can be seen as follows:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-vultisig/blob/main/src%2FILOPool.sol#L212-L227
```solidity
// Calculate fees generated by position
uint256 fees0 = FullMath.mulDiv(
    feeGrowthInside0LastX128 - position.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
    positionLiquidity,
    FixedPoint128.Q128
);

uint256 fees1 = FullMath.mulDiv(
    feeGrowthInside1LastX128 - position.feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
    positionLiquidity,
    FixedPoint128.Q128
);

// Amount of fees after deducting performance fee
(fees0, fees1) = _deductFees(fees0, fees1, _project.performanceFee);

```

If `_project.performanceFee` is set to 10000, then `fees0` and `fees1` after deduction would be 0. Therefore, the investor gets no profit from the generated fees. The same case for `platformFee`

## Tools Used

Manual code review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Define Maximum Fee Constants
    ```solidity
